title: Micro-hydro generator for a small stream
summary: Pipe water from higher up a stream down to a small turbine that spins a DC motor or alternator and charges a battery day and night. A stream with 10 m of fall and 2 L/s can give about 80–100W round the clock, about 2kWh a day, often far more than the same effort in solar. It needs a dump-load controller and daily care of the intake.

materials.item: Generator: treadmill motor (permanent-magnet DC) or a direct-drive washing-machine motor
Outer-rotor brushless motor (washing machine) as an alternative generator
Penstock pipe, 40–100 mm, long enough to reach from intake to turbine
Nozzle: a reducer or a drilled end cap, plus a shut-off valve
Runner: steel or aluminium disc 150–300 mm with 12–20 cups (cut pipe halves or spoons)
Shaft and two bearings, if not driving the generator directly
Belt and pulleys for a speed step-up
Bridge rectifier 25–35A (three, or a 3-phase bridge, for brushless motors)
Dump-load controller (relay or MOSFET with voltage trigger)
Dump load: power resistors, 12V bulbs or 12V heating elements, 1.5× generator peak
Fuse within 30 cm of battery +, sized to the cable
Cable from turbine to battery, sized for drop (see build_solar_12v_system)
Drums or boxes: one for the intake with a 2–6 mm mesh screen, one as the turbine housing (or build it from plywood or sheet steel)

steps.text: Measure flow in the dry season: dam a narrow spot with a board or pipe and time how long a 20 L bucket takes to fill. Flow (L/s) = 20 ÷ seconds. Plan to use no more than half of it.
steps.warn: Fast, cold water knocks people off their feet even when it's knee-deep. Work with a partner and wear grippy footwear.

steps.text: Measure head (fall) from intake to turbine site: run a hose full of water and measure pressure at the bottom (1 bar ≈ 10 m), or sight with a level and pole in steps. Then work out power with the notes. Under about 20W, solar is probably easier.
Pick a turbine. More than about 5 m of head and low flow: a Pelton-style wheel (cups hit by a jet). Under about 3 m of head with lots of flow: a waterwheel or propeller, slower and bulkier.

Build the intake in a pool above the turbine: a drum or box with a mesh screen, the pipe outlet a little above the bottom so silt settles out. Leave the stream able to flow past for fish and for people downstream.
Lay the penstock downhill without high points, where air gets trapped. Size it from the friction table in the notes so you lose under 10–15% of the head. Anchor or bury it.
steps.warn: A full pipe on a slope is heavy and can slide. Pipe sections and turbines are heavy to carry on steep banks.

steps.text: Fit a valve and the nozzle at the bottom. Size the nozzle from the notes; start a little small and drill bigger if pressure stays high.
steps.warn: Close valves slowly, over several seconds. Slamming a valve on a long pipe makes a pressure spike (water hammer) that bursts pipes and fittings.

steps.text: Make the runner: bolt 12–20 evenly spaced cups round a disc, each facing the jet with its split or centre ridge on the jet line. The jet should hit cups squarely and leave sideways.

Mount the runner on the generator shaft (or on its own shaft with bearings and a belt). Enclose it in a housing that catches spray and drains back to the stream. Keep the electrics dry and above flood level.

Wire: generator → rectifier → fuse at the battery → battery. Connect the dump-load controller and dump load across the battery. Set the dump load to switch on at 14.4V (see build_treadmill_wind_generator for a circuit).
steps.warn: Hydro runs day and night. Without a working dump load it overcharges and boils the battery, or overspeeds if disconnected. A boiling battery sprays acid and gives off explosive hydrogen; keep it ventilated.

steps.text: Open the valve slowly. Measure volts and amps. Try a different nozzle size or belt ratio to find the most watts; a Pelton runs best at about half its no-load speed.
Daily, especially in autumn: clear leaves from the intake screen. Monthly: grease bearings, check belts, flush silt from the intake and the bottom of the pipe.

notes:
## Power
Power (W) = 9.81 × flow (L/s) × net head (m) × efficiency. Home-built Pelton wheels on DC motors manage about 0.4–0.6.

| Flow | 3 m | 10 m | 20 m | 40 m |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 L/s | 6–9W | 20–30W | 40–60W | 80–120W |
| 2 L/s | 24–35W | 80–120W | 160–235W | 315–470W |
| 5 L/s | 60–90W | 200–295W | 390–590W | 785–1,180W |

Running 24 hours: 100W = 2.4kWh a day, about what 600–800W of solar panel gives on a good day.

## Measuring head with a hose
Fill a long hose, cap the bottom end with a pressure gauge, and put the open top end at the intake. Each bar on the gauge is about 10.2 m of head (each psi is about 0.7 m). On long runs, measure in stages.

## Pipe friction (metres lost per 100 m of smooth plastic pipe, inside diameter)
| Flow | 32 mm | 40 mm | 50 mm | 63 mm | 75 mm | 100 mm |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 L/s | 1.7 | 0.6 | 0.2 | – | – | – |
| 1 L/s | 6.0 | 2.0 | 0.7 | 0.2 | – | – |
| 2 L/s | – | 7.3 | 2.5 | 0.8 | 0.3 | – |
| 5 L/s | – | – | – | 4.4 | 1.9 | 0.5 |
| 10 L/s | – | – | – | – | 6.7 | 1.7 |

Net head = gross head − friction loss. Example: 100 m of 50 mm pipe at 2 L/s loses 2.5 m. On a 10 m head that's 25%: use 63 mm instead (0.8 m, 8%). Fittings and bends add a little more.

## Pelton sizing
- Jet speed (m/s) ≈ 4.3 × √(net head in m). 10 m → about 13.6 m/s.
- Nozzle diameter (mm) ≈ 1,000 × √(4 × flow in m³/s ÷ (π × jet speed)). 2 L/s at 10 m → about 14 mm. Two smaller jets on opposite sides also work.
- Best cup speed ≈ 0.46 × jet speed. Runner rpm = cup speed × 60 ÷ (π × runner diameter in m). A 0.2 m runner at 10 m head turns about 600 rpm.
- Generator: at 600 rpm a treadmill motor of 20–30V per 1,000 rpm gives 12–18V, right for a 12V battery. Otherwise change runner size or add a belt.

## Generators
- **Treadmill motors:** simple, brushed; brushes wear over months of 24-hour running, so carry spares.
- **Direct-drive washer motors:** brushless, run well at low rpm, output 3-phase AC (rectify). Rewiring the stator for low voltage is possible but needs care.
- **Car alternators:** need 1,500+ rpm and field current; workable on high heads only.

## Dump load
The battery fills; the water keeps coming. A dump load takes surplus power when the battery reaches about 14.4V. A water-heating element sized for 12V is a useful dump load: free hot water. See build_treadmill_wind_generator for a simple TL431 trigger circuit.

## Low head
A waterwheel 1–2 m across in a 0.5–1 m drop turns slowly (5–20 rpm) and needs big gearing, from bicycle sprockets and chain or belts. Expect tens of watts from a lot of building.

## Troubleshooting
- Power drops over days: intake screen clogging, air in the pipe, nozzle partly blocked.
- High pressure at the nozzle but low output: nozzle too small, or the jet misses the cup centres.
- Low pressure with the valve open: pipe too small, a leak, or an air lock at a high point.

## If you lack a part
- No pressure gauge: measure head with a level, a straight pole and a tape, in steps down the slope.
- No pipe: open channels lined with plastic sheet can carry water to a low-head wheel.
